items.readable_text:
Content:
When we reduce a matrix to row echelon form, the number of pivot columns plus the number of non-pivot columns always equals the total number of columns of the matrix.

Content:
By translating this into the language of vector spaces, we get the rank-nullity theorem. The rank-nullity theorem relates the rank of a matrix to the dimension of its null space:

Content:
> Let [MATH: A] be a matrix (not necessarily square) with [MATH: n] columns. Then,
> [MATH: \textrm{dim(Col}(A)) + \textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n),]
> or, equivalently,
> [MATH: \textrm{rank}(A) + \textrm{nullity}(A) = n.]

Content:
For example, suppose that for some matrix [MATH: A,] we have

Content:
[MATH: [− 2x_{2}; x_{2}; 2x_{3}; x_{2} − x_{3}]]

Content:
We can use the rank-nullity theorem to calculate [MATH: \textrm{rank}(A).]

Content:
In this case, we must have [MATH: n=4,] since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space.

Content:
Also, we must have [MATH: \textrm{nullity}(A)=2,] since
[MATH: [− 2; 1; 0; 1]]

Content:
Therefore, using the rank-nullity theorem, we have

Content:
[MATH: rank(A) + nullity(A)|= n; rank(A) + 2|= 4; rank(A)|= 4 − 2; = 2.]

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

[MATH: Col(A) = R^{3}; dim(Col(A)) = 3 = rank(A); Null(A) = {0}; dim(Null(A)) = 0 = nullity(A)]

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if [MATH: A] is a matrix with [MATH: n] columns, then

[MATH: \textrm{rank}(A) + \textrm{nullity}(A) = n.]

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that [MATH: [1; 0; 0]] which means that [MATH: \textrm{nullity}(A) =2.]

    Now, for the matrix [MATH: A,] the number of columns is [MATH: n = 3,] so according to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain [MATH: rank(A) + nullity(A)|= n; rank(A) + 2|= 3; rank(A)|= 3 − 2; = 1.]

  • Statement II is false. Since [MATH: \textrm{nullity}(A) = 2 \neq 0,] then by the invertible matrix theorem, [MATH: A] cannot be an invertible matrix.

  • Statement III is false. Since [MATH: \textrm{rank}(A) = 1,] we have that [MATH: \textrm{Col}(A)] is a [MATH: 1]-dimensional subspace of [MATH: \Bbb R^3.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When we reduce a matrix to row echelon form, the number of pivot columns plus the number of non-pivot columns always equals the total number of columns of the matrix.

Content:
By translating this into the language of vector spaces, we get the rank-nullity theorem. The rank-nullity theorem relates the rank of a matrix to the dimension of its null space:

Content:
> Let [MATH: A] be a matrix (not necessarily square) with [MATH: n] columns. Then,
> [MATH: \textrm{dim(Col}(A)) + \textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n),]
> or, equivalently,
> [MATH: \textrm{rank}(A) + \textrm{nullity}(A) = n.]

Content:
For example, suppose that for some matrix [MATH: A,] we have

Content:
[MATH: [− 2x_{2}; x_{2}; 2x_{3}; x_{2} − x_{3}]]

Content:
We can use the rank-nullity theorem to calculate [MATH: \textrm{rank}(A).]

Content:
In this case, we must have [MATH: n=4,] since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space.

Content:
Also, we must have [MATH: \textrm{nullity}(A)=2,] since
[MATH: [− 2; 1; 0; 1]]

Content:
Therefore, using the rank-nullity theorem, we have

Content:
[MATH: rank(A) + nullity(A)|= n; rank(A) + 2|= 4; rank(A)|= 4 − 2; = 2.]

---

For the given matrix, we have [MATH: n=6.] Therefore,
